posts.author: JensenHuang
posts.text: Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me. I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA. I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation. Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO. Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours. Jensen

posts.author: BenBakerMO
posts.text: Elon Musk says we've entered the Singularity. Here's what that actually means. This morning he posted: "Unequivocal super intelligence has arrived. Welcome to the Singularity." The trigger: a claimed AI-assisted proof of the Riemann hypothesis — one of math's oldest unsolved problems. But the proof is 17 million lines long, and independent mathematicians haven't verified it yet. Worth keeping in mind. What is the singularity? • The idea dates to 1965: a machine smart enough to design a smarter machine, until progress accelerates past human understanding • It's not robots taking over — it's the future becoming unpredictable, because the thing driving change is smarter than we are • Ray Kurzweil, who popularized the idea, still says 2045 Musk's timeline: • AI smarter than any individual human by end of 2026 or 2027 • Smarter than all of humanity combined by 2030-31 • White-collar information jobs hit first • Billions of robots doing physical work; goods and services "close to free" • The bottleneck isn't the algorithms — it's electricity and computing power He's not alone. Sam Altman agreed in July, Anthropic's Jack Clark told the IMF it started this year. DeepMind's Hassabis is more measured — he says we're "in the foothills." Musk's claim is less a measurement than a worldview: AI is now improving itself fast enough that the old pace of change is gone. Turning point, or just another impressive demo?

posts.author: brivael
posts.text: I don't think people realize what's happening with Elon Musk right now. Look at what he posted today. The CEO of the most valuable car company in the world explains, on a Sunday, on X, that his team had to fit the decoder of their world model into the chip's SRAM, that they only had half an accelerator to work with, that this accelerator only handles 8-bit integers, and that softmax has to be emulated in 28 steps. Name one other CEO at that level who could write that post. Not have it written. Write it. That's not a detail. I think the way Musk operates at scale, combined with superintelligence, is going to give him an absolutely insane edge. Let's go back to first principles. A company is a machine that turns intent into reality. Between the two, there are two costs. The intelligence needed to find the solution. And the synchronization needed to get thousands of people executing it in the same direction. Superintelligence is wiping out the first one. When thousands of agents smarter than your best engineers cost the price of electricity, intelligence is no longer scarce. That leaves the second one. And it's exploding. The bottleneck today is synchronization. Humans synchronizing agents. And humans synchronizing the humans who synchronize agents. Every layer is lossy compression. The CEO tells the VP, who rephrases it for the director, who rephrases it for the manager, who prompts the agent. By the end, the agent flawlessly executes an intent nobody recognizes anymore. Agents don't fix this. They amplify it. They move so fast that one bad intent turns into a thousand bad deliverables before the next leadership meeting. Now listen to Marc Andreessen. He broke down what he calls "the Elon method." Every week, at every company, Musk finds the single biggest bottleneck and fixes it himself. He doesn't ask the VP to ask the director to ask the manager. He goes straight to the engineer on the problem and solves it with them. The rest of the time, he runs engineering reviews where every engineer presents what they're building. Ben Horowitz, Andreessen's partner, sums up the condition that makes it almost impossible to copy: you need to be able to hold every engineering topic in the company in your head, all at the same time. Here's what almost nobody sees: the Elon method is exactly the architecture of the agent era. The shortest possible sync chain between the person who understands and the thing that executes. A CEO who doesn't understand what he's doing can only delegate his trust. A CEO who understands can delegate the work, and check the result. With humans, that gap cost months. With agents, it will cost orders of magnitude. Second edge: hardware. Superintelligence doesn't live in a vacuum. It needs chips, energy, data, and a body to act in the physical world. Musk has all of it. Millions of cars filming reality around the clock. His own chips. Compute through xAI. Energy storage. Robots with Optimus. Rockets and a satellite constellation. And look at how it all connects. The same vision encoder powers FSD, Robotaxi and Optimus. One intelligence, three bodies. The next-generation chip, AI5, goes straight into Optimus, because according to him AI4 is already enough to solve driving. Everyone else is optimizing a model. He's optimizing a full loop: data, training, silicon, energy, factory, robot, and back to data. Put the two together. Intelligence is becoming a commodity. What stays scarce is atoms and sync speed. Musk is probably the man on earth who owns the most of both. The labs have the models, not the factories. The industrials have the factories, not the models. The giants who have both have ten layers of management between the person who decides and the person who knows. I look at the map and I don't see anyone who can keep up in this configuration. Honestly, I don't even see how he loses. In the world that's coming, intelligence will be free. Understanding what you're doing will never be for sale.
